headings.title: Introduction to Skin Snip Procedure and Indications
headings.content: The **skin snip** is a minor surgical procedure performed primarily to diagnose specific subcutaneous and dermal parasitic infections. Most notably, it serves as the definitive diagnostic tool for **onchocerciasis**, commonly known as river blindness, caused by the filarial nematode *Onchocerca volvulus*. Microfilariae reside in the dermal layers of the skin, where they can be harvested via this targeted tissue sampling technique. Beyond onchocerciasis, healthcare providers occasionally utilize the skin snip to detect other dermal microfilariae such as *Mansonella streptocerca*. Recognizing the geographic distribution and clinical history of patients helps nurses anticipate when this diagnostic test is necessary. Patients presenting with chronic pruritus, skin depigmentation ("leopard skin"), subcutaneous nodules, or visual disturbances in endemic regions often require this evaluation.

headings.title: Patient Preparation and Safety Assessment
headings.content: Before performing a skin snip, the nurse must conduct a thorough safety assessment to minimize risks and ensure patient readiness. Assessing the patient's bleeding history is vital, especially if they take anticoagulants or have a bleeding disorder like hemophilia, because even superficial snips can cause prolonged bleeding. The nurse must also check for known allergies to local anesthetics such as lidocaine. Obtaining informed consent is a mandatory step; the nurse ensures the patient understands why the test is done, what sensations to expect, and potential minor discomfort. Selecting an appropriate anatomical site is another key preparatory duty. Common sites include the iliac crest, scapula, or gluteal region, depending on regional protocol and where nodules or microfilariae concentration are highest.

headings.title: Equipment and Sterile Technique Setup
headings.content:
A successful skin snip relies on maintaining strict sterile technique to prevent secondary bacterial infections. 

- **Antiseptic solution**: Chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine to cleanse the biopsy site.
- **Local anesthetic**: Lidocaine 1% or 2% without epinephrine, plus a small syringe and needle for intradermal injection.
- **Lifting tool**: A sterile needle (usually 25G or 27G) or a specialized corneo-scleral punch to elevate the tissue.
- **Cutting tool**: A sterile surgical scalpel (No. 11 blade) or a scleral punch instrument.
- **Transport medium**: Normal saline or distilled water in a microcentrifuge tube or watch glass to emerge the tissue.

The nurse organizes these supplies on a sterile field and ensures personal protective equipment is worn throughout the procedure.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedural Execution
headings.content: Executing a skin snip requires precision and steady hands from the clinician, supported by an attentive nurse. First, the chosen skin area is cleaned thoroughly with an antiseptic and allowed to dry. The clinician injects a small amount of local anesthetic to form a small skin wheal, minimizing patient discomfort. Once numbness is confirmed, a sterile needle is inserted horizontally just beneath the epidermis to lift a tiny cone of skin, roughly 1 to 2 millimeters in diameter. Using a sharp scalpel blade or a sclerotome punch, the clinician snips off the elevated skin bleb just above the needle level. The goal is to obtain a superficial piece of dermis without causing deep subcutaneous bleeding. The nurse immediately transfers the tiny tissue specimen into a collection vessel containing sterile saline or water.

headings.title: Specimen Handling and Laboratory Examination
headings.content: Proper handling of the skin snip specimen ensures accurate diagnostic results and prevents sample degradation or loss. Once placed in the liquid medium (saline or distilled water), the vial is left at room temperature for a designated incubation period, typically ranging from 30 minutes to several hours, or even overnight depending on laboratory protocol. Over this period, live microfilariae actively migrate out of the tissue tissue matrix and into the surrounding fluid. The nurse or laboratory technician then examines the liquid sediment using a low-power microscope or transfers it to a slide for staining and counting. Clear labeling of the specimen container with patient identifiers and anatomical collection sites is critical to prevent diagnostic errors.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Wound Care and Complication Management
headings.content: Although a skin snip is minor, proper post-procedure care prevents infection and promotes quick healing. After tissue collection, direct pressure is applied to the small biopsy site using sterile gauze until any minor bleeding completely stops. The nurse then cleans the site gently and applies a sterile adhesive bandage. Patient education focuses on keeping the wound clean and dry for at least 24 hours. The nurse instructs the patient to report signs of infection such as spreading redness, warmth, swelling, or purulent drainage. Complications are rare but can include localized hematoma, mild pain, or secondary bacterial infection. Reassurance regarding minor, transient tenderness at the site helps alleviate unnecessary worry.
